We test language models' ability to match conditional probabilities with and without intermediate reasoning steps, finding that intermediate steps are only helpful when the training data is locally structured with respect to dependencies between variables. The combination of locally structured observations and reasoning is much more data-efficient than training on all variables. Our results illustrate how the effectiveness of reasoning step by step is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.

papers.title: Emergence of symbolic abstraction heads for in-context learning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do small transformer models recognize, learn, and generalize abstract sequential symbolic patterns, and do they form internal symbolic representations through abstraction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Small transformer models can learn abstract symbolic patterns and develop abstraction heads for in-context learning, enabling symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Small transformer models can recognize and generalize abstract patterns through abstraction heads, providing insights for neuro-symbolic processing.
papers.key_findings:
Models with 2 or 3 layers successfully solve abstract pattern matching tasks, while 1-layer models fail.
Abstraction heads emerge in attention mechanisms, attending to the first instantiation to generalize patterns.
Variable matching is a simpler task that can be solved even by single-layer models without abstraction.
Training loss shows bumps that correlate with sudden improvements in accuracy, indicating learning of critical strategies.
Abstraction heads operate at a more abstract level than induction heads, focusing on pattern matching from instantiations.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are based on simplified sequences of numbers and may not generalize to human language or complex relations.
The study is limited to small transformer models with 1-3 layers, and different mechanisms may emerge in larger models.
future_direction: Investigate alternative mechanisms for abstract pattern matching in transformers.
Explore the emergence of abstraction heads in larger models with more layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on self-attention circuits are able to perform, at inference time, novel reasoning tasks, but the mechanisms inside the models are currently not fully understood. We assume that LLMs are able to generalize abstract patterns from the input and form an internal symbolic internal representation of the content. In this paper, we study this by analyzing the performance of small LLM models trained with sequences of instantiations of abstract sequential symbolic patterns or templates. It is shown that even a model with two layers is able to learn an abstract template and use it to generate correct output representing the pattern. This can be seen as a form of symbolic inference taking place inside the network. In this paper, we call the emergent mechanism abstraction head. Identifying mechanisms of symbolic reasoning in a neural network can help to find new ways to merge symbolic and neural processing.

papers.title: Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their Chain-of-Thought?
papers.research_question: How robust are reasoning LLMs to interventions on their chain-of-thought?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controlled benchmark to evaluate the robustness of reasoning LLMs to interventions on their chain-of-thought, finding that models are generally robust but with trade-offs in efficiency and style invariance.
papers.conclusion: The findings clarify how RLLMs maintain reasoning integrity under disruptions, reveal trade-offs between robustness and compute cost, and point to training targets for improving recovery strategies.
papers.key_findings:
RLLMs are generally robust to interventions, with robustness improving with model size.
Robustness degrades when interventions occur early in the chain-of-thought.
Paraphrasing interventions suppress doubt-like expressions and reduce performance.
Doubt expressions play a central role in recovery from perturbations.
Neutral and adversarial noise can inflate CoT length by over 200%, while paraphrasing shortens traces but harms accuracy.
future_direction: preserving appropriate doubt
improving style robustness
developing recovery strategies that control token cost
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) generate step-by-step chains of thought (CoTs) before giving an answer, which improves performance on complex tasks and makes reasoning more transparent. But how robust are these reasoning traces to disruptions that occur within them? To address this question, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that perturbs a model's own CoT at fixed timesteps. We design seven interventions (benign, neutral, and adversarial) and apply them to multiple open-weight RLLMs across Math, Science, and Logic tasks. Our results show that RLLMs are generally robust, reliably recovering from diverse perturbations, with robustness improving with model size and degrading when interventions occur early. However, robustness is not style-invariant: paraphrasing suppresses doubt-like expressions and reduces performance, while other interventions trigger doubt and support recovery. Recovery also carries a cost: neutral and adversarial noise can inflate CoT length by more than 200%, whereas paraphrasing shortens traces but harms accuracy. These findings provide new evidence on how RLLMs maintain reasoning integrity, identify doubt as a central recovery mechanism, and highlight trade-offs between robustness and efficiency that future training methods should address.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Do Latent-CoT Models Think Step-by-Step? A Mechanistic Study on Sequential Reasoning Tasks
papers.research_question: Does latent chain-of-thought (specifically CODI) implement genuine step-by-step reasoning on sequential tasks, or does it rely on shortcuts and late-stage fusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent CoT (CODI) implements step-by-step reasoning only for short hops (2-3) and shifts to a partial, late-bottleneck strategy for longer tasks, with performance and mechanism depending on the compressibility of the task (composite vs prime moduli).
papers.conclusion: With composite moduli, CODI is step-by-step on 2–3 hops but shifts to a late-intermediate partial rollout on longer horizons; with prime moduli, it largely fails to learn and shows neither signature. The split is explained by compressibility: composite moduli induce many-to-one contractions that bias the label toward late updates, making the computation compressible, while prime moduli lack this structure.
papers.key_findings:
For 2-3 hop polynomial tasks, CODI forms bridge states in the latent channel and fuses them with the final input at the answer readout.
For longer hop tasks (n>=4), CODI collapses to a partial latent rollout, representing only the last one or two intermediate states.
There is a prime-composite split: under composite moduli, CODI succeeds with a late-bottleneck strategy; under prime moduli, performance drops and step-by-step reasoning fails.
The final input is routed directly to the answer readout via a copy-like pathway, separate from the latent channel.
Teacher-guided compression drives the partial-reasoning strategy under composite moduli.
papers.limitation: CODI struggles with incompressible sequential tasks (e.g., prime moduli) due to fixed latent-compute budget.
future_direction: Test whether the compressibility dependence (including the prime–composite split) persists across latent-CoT objectives and architectures.
Develop adaptive mechanisms that allocate latent compute to match task demands.
Extend the mechanistic toolbox to more sequential and naturalistic datasets.
papers.abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought (Latent-CoT) aims to enable step-by-step computation without emitting long rationales, yet its mechanisms remain unclear. We study CODI, a continuous-thought teacher-student distillation model, on strictly sequential polynomial-iteration tasks. Using logit-lens decoding, linear probes, attention analysis, and activation patching, we localize intermediate-state representations and trace their routing to the final readout. On two- and three-hop tasks, CODI forms the full set of bridge states that become decodable across latent-thought positions, while the final input follows a separate near-direct route; predictions arise via late fusion at the end-of-thought boundary. For longer hop lengths, CODI does not reliably execute a full latent rollout, instead exhibiting a partial latent reasoning path that concentrates on late intermediates and fuses them with the last input at the answer readout position. Ablations show that this partial pathway can collapse under regime shifts, including harder optimization. Overall, we delineate when CODI-style latent-CoT yields faithful iterative computation versus compressed or shortcut strategies, and highlight challenges in designing robust latent-CoT objectives for sequential reasoning.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Fluid Representations in Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How do reasoning language models internally process abstract structural information, and do they dynamically construct new representations during problem-solving?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning models dynamically refine internal representations of actions and predicates during extended reasoning, and these refined representations causally improve problem-solving performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that reasoning models' superior performance on abstract reasoning tasks may stem from their ability to dynamically construct context-specific representational spaces during extended reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
QwQ-32B progressively adapts internal representations of actions and predicates during reasoning, converging toward consistent encodings regardless of initial action names.
These representational adaptations causally improve problem-solving performance: injecting refined representations from successful traces boosts accuracy.
Adapted representations achieve symbolic abstraction, enabling cross-naming transfer and minimal performance loss when replaced with symbolic representations.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single reasoning model (QwQ-32B) and a single domain (BlocksWorld).
Steering and patching intervention methods are deliberately simple and coarse.
Computational limits prevented extensive hyperparameter sweeps or decoding strategy comparisons.
future_direction: Verifying generalization to other structured planning setups and less constrained domains.
Using more targeted or fine-grained causal tools.
Explaining late-layer representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models, which generate long chains of thought, dramatically outperform non-reasoning language models on abstract problems. However, the internal model mechanisms that allow this superior performance remain poorly understood. We present a mechanistic analysis of how QwQ-32B - a model specifically trained to produce extensive reasoning traces - process abstract structural information. On Mystery Blocksworld - a semantically obfuscated planning domain - we find that QwQ-32B gradually improves its internal representation of actions and concepts during reasoning. The model develops abstract encodings that focus on structure rather than specific action names. Through steering experiments, we establish causal evidence that these adaptations improve problem solving: injecting refined representations from successful traces boosts accuracy, while symbolic representations can replace many obfuscated encodings with minimal performance loss. We find that one of the factors driving reasoning model performance is in-context refinement of token representations, which we dub Fluid Reasoning Representations.

papers.title: From Explicit CoT to Implicit CoT: Learning to Internalize CoT Step by Step
papers.research_question: Can language models be taught to internalize chain-of-thought reasoning steps, thereby simplifying the reasoning process while maintaining high performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Stepwise Internalization, a method to internalize chain-of-thought reasoning by gradually removing intermediate steps during training, enabling models to achieve high accuracy without explicit CoT generation.
papers.conclusion: Stepwise Internalization enables implicit CoT reasoning, achieving high accuracy and faster inference compared to explicit CoT, and demonstrates the potential of internalizing reasoning steps in language models.
papers.key_findings:
Stepwise Internalization enables a GPT-2 Small model to solve 9-by-9 multiplication with up to 99% accuracy, whereas standard training fails beyond 4-by-4 multiplication.
On GSM8K, Stepwise Internalization achieves over 50% accuracy with Mistral 7B without explicit CoT, outperforming GPT-4 without CoT (44%).
Stepwise Internalization lags behind explicit CoT in accuracy but is faster, achieving up to 11x speedup on 9x9 multiplication.
The method allows trading off accuracy and speed by internalizing different amounts of CoT tokens.
Ablation studies show the importance of removal smoothing and optimizer reset for stable training.
papers.limitation:
High training cost due to finetuning required when removing each set of CoT tokens.
Instability of training with aggressive removal schedules, which can lead to non-convergence.
Loss of interpretable intermediate steps, similar to existing No CoT and implicit CoT training.
Accuracy still lags behind explicit CoT, though it offers a trade-off between latency and accuracy.
future_direction: Probing the internal processes as the model internalizes each reasoning step to provide insights into learning mechanisms.
Developing a mixed-mode approach that combines implicit and explicit CoT reasoning to balance accuracy, latency, and interpretability.
Scaling Stepwise Internalization to larger models and more extensive training/pretraining setups to enhance effectiveness on a broader range of reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: When leveraging language models for reasoning tasks, generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) steps often proves essential for achieving high accuracy in final outputs. In this paper, we investigate if models can be taught to internalize these CoT steps. To this end, we propose a simple yet effective method for internalizing CoT steps: starting with a model trained for explicit CoT reasoning, we gradually remove the intermediate steps and finetune the model. This process allows the model to internalize the intermediate reasoning steps, thus simplifying the reasoning process while maintaining high performance. Our approach enables a GPT-2 Small model to solve 9-by-9 multiplication with up to 99% accuracy, whereas standard training cannot solve beyond 4-by-4 multiplication. Furthermore, our method proves effective on larger language models, such as Mistral 7B, achieving over 50% accuracy on GSM8K without producing any intermediate steps.

papers.title: Towards Determining How Deep Neural Models Learn to Reason
papers.research_question: Can deep neural models learn to reason (deductive reasoning) in the absence of memorization and semantic shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a recurrent neural network trained from scratch on synthetic propositional logic formulas can achieve high accuracy in classifying theorems vs. non-theorems, suggesting that deep neural models can learn reasoning strategies without relying on memorization or semantic shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: The binary classification model is an exploratory first step towards a generative transformer-based model for theorem proving, and future work will apply mechanistic interpretability to understand learned reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The RNN classifier achieves up to 99.4% accuracy on the binary classification task of determining if a propositional formula is a theorem or non-theorem.
Performance suggests the model learns reasoning strategies rather than memorizing patterns or using semantic shortcuts.
Models with more hidden units (e.g., 128) achieve higher accuracy.
papers.limitation: The authors state that with the presented results, they cannot assert that the model has actually learned logical reasoning rules, only that it performs well on accuracy metrics.
future_direction: Generalize the approach from propositional logic to first-order logic.
Develop a generative deep transformer-based model trained on proof steps, not just binary labels.
Apply mechanistic interpretability techniques, specifically feature circuits, to analyze models trained on the synthetic data.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are well known to perform poorly on tasks involving reasoning, including deductive, inductive, abductive, and spatial reasoning. This is evidenced by many existing benchmarks. While techniques such as chain-of-thought prompting and inference computation attempt to improve reasoning performance, it is necessary to assess whether large models are ultimately "memorizing" answers to the questions being used to assess their purportedly learnt reasoning capabilities. In this short paper, we describe a work in progress that aims to investigate the innate reasoning processes of large models by generating new questions that require deductive reasoning to answer. Initially, we train from scratch and then assess the ability of a recurrent deep neural model to make such a binary decision. We then discuss how our preliminary results bear on the hypothesis that some deep neural models can indeed learn to reason in the absence of memorization and semantic shortcuts, and conclude by discussing future work.

papers.title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
papers.research_question: Do latent tokens in Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT) actually encode reasoning, or do they merely simulate the appearance of it?
papers.core_contribution: Latent tokens in COCONUT function as uninterpretable placeholders and promote shortcut usage, rather than encoding faithful reasoning, leading to inflated benchmark performance without true reasoning.
papers.conclusion: COCONUT tokens serve as pseudo-reasoning placeholders, are not semantically interpretable, and exhibit shortcut behaviors, indicating that latent reasoning in COCONUT is not faithful.
papers.key_findings:
COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering perturbations (PSR <5%) compared to CoT tokens (PSR up to 50%), indicating they lack reasoning-critical information.
Token-swapping experiments show COCONUT's accuracy remains stable after swapping, while CoT's drops, indicating latent tokens have limited influence on final predictions.
COCONUT exhibits strong shortcut dependence, e.g., in MMLU with biased options, incorrect predictions selecting the biased option rise to 70%.
In HotpotQA, COCONUT shows extreme sensitivity to shortcut manipulation, with accuracy dropping to near 0% when shortcuts favor incorrect answers.
PCA visualizations show latent token embeddings are distributed far from the main vocabulary manifold, indicating they act as placeholders without semantic meaning.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not establish a formal causal link between latent representations and reasoning quality.
The study did not deeply investigate the reasons why COCONUT relies on shortcuts, so the analysis remains speculative.
future_direction: Investigate more challenging out-of-distribution evaluations.
Design reasoning-specialized LLM baselines.
Develop novel interpretability metrics to probe latent reasoning traces.
papers.abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Abstraction-of-Thought Makes Language Models Better Reasoners
papers.research_question: How to elicit language models to reason with abstraction, and whether abstraction helps language models in reasoning.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Abstraction-of-Thought (AoT) reasoning format and a corresponding finetuning dataset (AOT COLLECTION), demonstrating that aligning models with AoT improves their reasoning performance compared to Chain-of-Thought.
papers.conclusion: Abstraction-of-Thought makes language models better reasoners, highlighting the potential of abstraction in enhancing model reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
AoT-finetuned models substantially outperform CoT-finetuned models on the Big-Bench Hard benchmark, especially on algorithmic tasks.
The AoT format, which requires explicit abstraction levels in reasoning, elicits better abstract reasoning in language models.
AoT-finetuning leads to significant improvements in zero-shot and few-shot performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation: The data collection process might not guarantee to find the optimal abstraction solution for each question, as the optimal abstraction level may differ across questions and a single question may have multiple abstract solutions.

papers.title: Understanding and Patching Compositional Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: What accounts for compositional reasoning failures in LLMs, and which parts of the LLMs are responsible for them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CREME, a model-editing method that patches compositional reasoning errors by editing MHSA modules, based on the finding that implicit reasoning results are generated and leveraged in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: Successful compositional reasoning within LLMs hinges on its awareness of generating and leveraging implicit reasoning results, and MHSA modules in middle layers are responsible for this process. The proposed CREME method effectively patches such errors.
papers.key_findings:
Most compositional reasoning failures stem from improperly generated or leveraged implicit reasoning results.
Implicit reasoning results emerge in middle layers and causally affect explicit reasoning results.
MHSA modules in middle layers (e.g., 18/19-th layer) are responsible for generating and leveraging implicit reasoning results.
CREME effectively patches compositional reasoning errors and generalizes to paraphrased and related queries.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Logit Lens, which is an approximate tool for interpreting hidden states.
Experiments are limited to 3B and 7B scale LLMs due to computational constraints.
Focus is on compositional reasoning of factual knowledge, not other task types.
future_direction: Validate conclusions on LLMs of larger scale.
Extend analysis to other types of compositional reasoning tasks, such as arithmetic reasoning.
papers.abstract: LLMs have marked a revolutonary shift, yet they falter when faced with compositional reasoning tasks. Our research embarks on a quest to uncover the root causes of compositional reasoning failures of LLMs, uncovering that most of them stem from the improperly generated or leveraged implicit reasoning results. Inspired by our empirical findings, we resort to Logit Lens and an intervention experiment to dissect the inner hidden states of LLMs. This deep dive reveals that implicit reasoning results indeed surface within middle layers and play a causative role in shaping the final explicit reasoning results. Our exploration further locates multi-head self-attention (MHSA) modules within these layers, which emerge as the linchpins in accurate generation and leveraing of implicit reasoning results. Grounded on the above findings, we develop CREME, a lightweight method to patch errors in compositional reasoning via editing the located MHSA modules. Our empirical evidence stands testament to CREME's effectiveness, paving the way for autonomously and continuously enhancing compositional reasoning capabilities in language models.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Fantastic Reasoning Behaviors and Where to Find Them: Unsupervised Discovery of the Reasoning Process
papers.research_question: How can we discover reasoning behaviors in large language models without human supervision, and can these discovered behaviors be used to controllably steer reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RISE, an unsupervised framework that uses sparse auto-encoders to discover reasoning vectors in LLM activations, enabling interpretation and control of reasoning behaviors without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The unsupervised framework RISE successfully discovers and enables control of reasoning behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable approach for interpretability and test-time adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
SAE decoder columns form clusters corresponding to human-interpretable reasoning behaviors such as reflection and backtracking.
Interventions on SAE-derived vectors can controllably amplify or suppress specific reasoning behaviors during inference without retraining.
SAEs capture structural properties of reasoning, such as response length, with clear separation in mid-to-late layers.
SAEs can discover novel behaviors not predefined by humans, such as confidence-related vectors that influence reasoning style.
The learned reasoning vectors generalize across different data domains (e.g., from math to commonsense reasoning).
future_direction: Scalable unsupervised discovery of reasoning behaviors.
Dynamic test-time adaptation using discovered vectors.
Alignment of structural and semantic features for reliable reasoning.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing reasoning capabilities of recent large language models (LLMs), their internal mechanisms during the reasoning process remain underexplored. Prior approaches often rely on human-defined concepts (e.g., overthinking, reflection) at the word level to analyze reasoning in a supervised manner. However, such methods are limited, as it is infeasible to capture the full spectrum of potential reasoning behaviors, many of which are difficult to define in token space. In this work, we propose an unsupervised framework (namely, RISE: Reasoning behavior Interpretability via Sparse auto-Encoder) for discovering reasoning vectors, which we define as directions in the activation space that encode distinct reasoning behaviors. By segmenting chain-of-thought traces into sentence-level 'steps' and training sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) on step-level activations, we uncover disentangled features corresponding to interpretable behaviors such as reflection and backtracking. Visualization and clustering analyses show that these behaviors occupy separable regions in the decoder column space. Moreover, targeted interventions on SAE-derived vectors can controllably amplify or suppress specific reasoning behaviors, altering inference trajectories without retraining. Beyond behavior-specific disentanglement, SAEs capture structural properties such as response length, revealing clusters of long versus short reasoning traces. More interestingly, SAEs enable the discovery of novel behaviors beyond human supervision. We demonstrate the ability to control response confidence by identifying confidence-related vectors in the SAE decoder space. These findings underscore the potential of unsupervised latent discovery for both interpreting and controllably steering reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Comprehension Without Competence: Architectural Limits of LLMs in Symbolic Computation and Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency, despite being able to fluently explain the correct principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes a fundamental architectural limitation in LLMs termed the 'computational split-brain syndrome,' where models can explain principles they cannot reliably execute, due to geometric separation of instruction and execution pathways.
papers.conclusion: LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning, and fundamental architectural innovations are needed to overcome these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a systematic gap between comprehension (explaining principles) and competence (executing them), termed computational split-brain syndrome.
This gap is rooted in architectural constraints: token embeddings resist domain binding, FFNs cannot implement exact symbolic operations, and next-token prediction decouples instruction from execution.
The syndrome manifests across domains (arithmetic and relational reasoning) and is not resolved by scaling or prompting.
Compensatory strategies (self-scaffolding, tool delegation, hybrid architectures) are necessary but highlight the need for metacognitive capabilities that current architectures lack.
Mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles.
papers.limitation:
Focus on pretrained transformer-based LLMs without external tools or explicit reasoning scaffolds.
Empirical evaluation centers on specific model families (LLaMA2, Claude, GPT-4) and may not generalize to fundamentally different architectures.
Geometric separation experiments rely on t-SNE projections which may not capture all relevant representational structure.
Theoretical analysis of FFN computational limits focuses on ReLU networks and may not apply to other activation functions.
future_direction: Developing future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution.
Empirical validation of the hypothesis that similar constraints apply to architectural variations like mixture-of-experts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) display striking surface fluency yet systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency. This paper offers a structural diagnosis of such failures, revealing a persistent gap between \textit{comprehension} and \textit{competence}. Through controlled experiments and architectural analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs often articulate correct principles without reliably applying them--a failure rooted not in knowledge access, but in computational execution. We term this phenomenon the computational \textit{split-brain syndrome}, where instruction and action pathways are geometrically and functionally dissociated. This core limitation recurs across domains, from mathematical operations to relational inferences, and explains why model behavior remains brittle even under idealized prompting. We argue that LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines, but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning. Our findings delineate the boundary of current LLM capabilities and motivate future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution. This diagnosis also clarifies why mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles, and why the geometric separation between instruction and execution pathways suggests limitations in neural introspection and mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
