Moreover, the effective reconstruction of multimodal reasoning processes with Heima Decoder validates both the robustness and interpretability of our approach.

papers.title: Demystifying Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the key factors that enable models to generate long chain-of-thought trajectories, and how can training strategies be optimized to enhance long CoT reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates the mechanics of long chain-of-thought reasoning, identifying key factors such as reward shaping and verifiable signals, and provides practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning, emphasizing the importance of reward shaping, verifiable signals, and careful design choices.
papers.key_findings:
SFT with long CoT scales to a higher performance upper limit than short CoT and facilitates further RL improvement.
Reasoning capabilities emerge with increased training compute, but reward shaping is crucial for stabilizing CoT length growth.
Scaling verifiable reward signals is critical for RL, and noisy web-extracted solutions with filtering show promise for out-of-distribution tasks.
Core abilities like error correction are inherently present in base models, but effective incentivization via RL demands significant compute.
The introduced Cosine Reward with repetition penalty can stabilize CoT length scaling and improve accuracy.
papers.limitation:
RL infrastructure is still in its infancy, with challenges in scaling to larger models due to hardware limitations and low utilization.
Smaller models may struggle to develop high-level reasoning skills and instead rely on heuristic-based pattern recognition.
Designing rule-based verifiers and curating prompt sets across different domains remains labor-intensive.
future_direction: Investigate RL using a larger base model.
Advancements in machine learning and systems research to overcome hardware limitations and accelerate progress in long CoT modeling.
Future research on silver supervision signals and self-supervised approaches in RL verification.
papers.abstract: Scaling inference compute enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs), with long chains-of-thought (CoTs) enabling strategies like backtracking and error correction. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial method for developing these capabilities, yet the conditions under which long CoTs emerge remain unclear, and RL training requires careful design choices. In this study, we systematically investigate the mechanics of long CoT reasoning, identifying the key factors that enable models to generate long CoT trajectories. Through extensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL experiments, we present four main findings: (1) While SFT is not strictly necessary, it simplifies training and improves efficiency; (2) Reasoning capabilities tend to emerge with increased training compute, but their development is not guaranteed, making reward shaping crucial for stabilizing CoT length growth; (3) Scaling verifiable reward signals is critical for RL. We find that leveraging noisy, web-extracted solutions with filtering mechanisms shows strong potential, particularly for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks such as STEM reasoning; and (4) Core abilities like error correction are inherently present in base models, but incentivizing these skills effectively for complex tasks via RL demands significant compute, and measuring their emergence requires a nuanced approach. These insights provide practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning in LLMs. Our code is available at: https://github.com/eddycmu/demystify-long-cot.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: S3-CoT: Self-Sampled Succinct Reasoning Enables Efficient Chain-of-Thought LLMs
papers.research_question: Can LLMs acquire a 'fast-thinking' mode analogous to human System 1 reasoning for efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) learning, and how can we obtain high-quality, variable-length CoT data without any teacher guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a self-sampling framework (S3-CoT) based on activation steering to sample variable-length, high-quality CoT data from target LLMs themselves, enabling efficient CoT internalization via SFT with a dual-cognitive system and progressive compression curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The S3-CoT framework successfully samples high-quality, variable-length CoT data from LLMs themselves and enables efficient CoT internalization via SFT, offering an early exploration of LLM self-evolution for reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies a variable-length direction (VL-D) in LLM representation space that governs CoT length and can be used for activation steering to sample variable-length CoT traces.
Self-sampled data via VL-D intervention produces style-aligned, variable-length CoT without external teacher guidance, with self-consistency verification ensuring high correctness.
SFT with self-sampled data and a progressive compression curriculum yields efficient CoT LLMs that compress reasoning length while maintaining or improving accuracy on math and medical benchmarks.
The method outperforms SFT-based baselines and is competitive with RL-based methods while using fewer training resources, and shows strong adaptability across general and R1-style LLMs.
Training exclusively on the shortest CoT samples leads to over-compression and accuracy degradation, justifying the need for a progressive curriculum.
papers.limitation: For R1-style LLMs, both our method and existing methods still face the challenge of slight accuracy degradation when compressing CoT length.
future_direction: Better leverage sampled data to push beyond the length–performance Pareto frontier.
Explore integration of SFT-based methods as a warm-start (pre-training) stage before RL to potentially yield additional performance gains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) equipped with chain-of-thought (CoT) achieve strong performance and offer a window into LLM behavior. However, recent evidence suggests that improvements in CoT capabilities often come with redundant reasoning processes, motivating a key question: Can LLMs acquire a fast-thinking mode analogous to human System 1 reasoning? To explore this, our study presents a self-sampling framework based on activation steering for efficient CoT learning. Our method can induce style-aligned and variable-length reasoning traces from target LLMs themselves without any teacher guidance, thereby alleviating a central bottleneck of SFT-based methods-the scarcity of high-quality supervision data. Using filtered data by gold answers, we perform SFT for efficient CoT learning with (i) a human-like dual-cognitive system, and (ii) a progressive compression curriculum. Furthermore, we explore a self-evolution regime in which SFT is driven solely by prediction-consistent data of variable-length variants, eliminating the need for gold answers. Extensive experiments on math benchmarks, together with cross-domain generalization tests in medicine, show that our method yields stable improvements for both general and R1-style LLMs. Our data and model checkpoints can be found at https://github.com/DYR1/S3-CoT.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: Parrot Mind: Towards Explaining the Complex Task Reasoning of Pretrained Large Language Models with Template-Content Structure
papers.research_question: How can pretrained large language models learn to solve complex reasoning tasks with limited training data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the template-content structure (T-C structure) as an intrinsic constraint in language that reduces the learning space from exponential to linear, explaining how LLMs can generalize on complex reasoning tasks with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The template-content structure provides a plausible explanation for how LLMs acquire complex reasoning abilities through language modeling, and empirical evidence supports its existence in current models.
papers.key_findings:
The T-C structure exists in current LLMs, as evidenced by lower variance in template token outputs compared to content tokens.
The T-C structure reduces the hypothesis space from exponential to linear, enabling within-task generalization.
Hierarchical T-C structure further reduces the space to logarithmic, enabling task composition across sub-tasks.
Larger models exhibit clearer T-C structure, with higher AUC in classifying template vs. content tokens.
The T-C structure explains how LLMs can perform reasoning through language modeling (parroting) by learning and reusing templates.
papers.limitation:
The T-C structure may not hold for all tasks, such as purely natural language tasks like translation or chatting.
The assumption of token-wise alignment is a simplification; semantic alignment is more realistic but introduces challenges.
The framework assumes deterministic generation, while practical models output probability distributions and use sampling.
future_direction: Extending the framework to handle sampling and probability distributions.
Investigating the disentanglement of semantic and position information in Transformers.
Applying the T-C structure to more complex tasks and real-world scenarios.
papers.abstract: The pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown their extraordinary capacity to solve reasoning tasks, even on tasks that require a complex process involving multiple sub-steps. However, given the vast possible generation space of all the tasks, how the pretrained model learns the reasoning ability remains an open question. We firstly propose that an intrinsic structural constraint on the generated sequence of language-based reasoning -- we called it template-content structure (T-C structure) -- is the key to explain why LLMs can solve a large number of complex reasoning problems with limited training data by showing this structure can reduce the possible space from exponential level to linear level. Furthermore, by generalizing this structure to the hierarchical case, we demonstrate that models can achieve task composition, further reducing the space needed to learn from linear to logarithmic, thereby effectively learning on complex reasoning involving multiple steps. We provide both examples and formal theory of our T-C structure. We also experimentally validate the existence of the T-C structure in some current LLMs and its effectiveness for reasoning.

papers.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought as Planning: Decoupling Reasoning from Verbalization
papers.research_question: How can we decouple reasoning from verbalization in latent reasoning, and model reasoning as planning in latent space to achieve dynamic termination and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PLaT, a framework that decouples reasoning from verbalization, enabling dynamic termination and interpretability of latent states, and shows a trade-off between greedy accuracy and reasoning diversity.
papers.conclusion: PLaT offers a transparent and scalable foundation for inference-time search by learning a broad solution manifold, shifting the focus from memorizing golden traces to learning generalizable search spaces.
papers.key_findings:
PLaT achieves lower greedy accuracy but higher reasoning diversity (Pass@k) compared to baselines.
PLaT's latent space supports efficient sampling of diverse answers, while baselines show saturation at higher k.
PLaT maintains a higher branching factor (diversity) throughout the reasoning process compared to explicit CoT.
Reinforcement learning on PLaT improves greedy accuracy on in-domain tasks but may overfit and degrade on out-of-domain tasks.
The decoupling allows for efficient inference via lazy decoding, skipping intermediate token generation.
papers.limitation:
The current Reinforcement Learning exploration is preliminary, with the Planner frozen and optimization restricted to the Decoder.
The scaling laws of latent states remain to be fully characterized, with performance saturation beyond a certain number of latent steps.
Evaluation is concentrated on mathematical reasoning; efficacy in less-structured domains remains to be validated.
future_direction: Investigate joint optimization strategies or iterative updates to refine the Planner alongside the Decoder in RL.
Unlock the potential of deeper latent trajectories with advanced training techniques.
Extend the paradigm to a broader spectrum of tasks such as creative writing, common-sense reasoning, or complex code generation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex problems, but remains constrained by the computational cost and reasoning path collapse when grounded in discrete token spaces. Recent latent reasoning approaches attempt to optimize efficiency by performing reasoning within continuous hidden states. However, these methods typically operate as opaque end-to-end mappings from explicit reasoning steps to latent states, and often require a pre-defined number of latent steps during inference. In this work, we introduce PLaT (Planning with Latent Thoughts), a framework that reformulates latent reasoning as planning by fundamentally decouple reasoning from verbalization. We model reasoning as a deterministic trajectory of latent planning states, while a separate Decoder grounds these thoughts into text when necessary. This decoupling allows the model to dynamically determine when to terminate reasoning rather than relying on fixed hyperparameters. Empirical results on mathematical benchmarks reveal a distinct trade-off: while PLaT achieves lower greedy accuracy than baselines, it demonstrates superior scalability in terms of reasoning diversity. This indicates that PLaT learns a robust, broader solution space, offering a transparent and scalable foundation for inference-time search. Our code can be found in https://github.com/yunsaijc/PLaT.

papers.title: On the Bias of Next-Token Predictors Toward Systematically Inefficient Reasoning: A Shortest-Path Case Study
papers.research_question: How does the efficiency and structure of reasoning traces (e.g., optimal dynamic programming vs. inefficient backtracking) affect the generalization and next-token prediction confidence of transformers trained on shortest-path tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers trained on inefficient, systematic reasoning traces (with backtracking) generalize better than those trained on optimal dynamic programming traces, due to higher next-token prediction confidence.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that chain-of-thought is crucial for generalization, that structured but inefficient reasoning traces are more effective than globally optimal ones, and that next-token confidence predicts learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Training with intermediate reasoning traces (chain-of-thought) substantially improves generalization compared to direct question-answer training.
Models trained on inefficient depth-first search traces outperform those trained on optimal dynamic programming traces, even when trace lengths are equalized.
The benefit of inefficient traces is not due to length alone; injecting arbitrary redundancy without systematic structure can hurt performance.
Generalization correlates with next-token confidence: traces that are more predictable (systematic and locally incremental) yield higher confidence and better learning.
Models exhibit a bias towards generating longer traces, which can be regularized by sampling at non-zero temperature.
papers.limitation: The synthetic algorithmic task and custom token language may limit transferability to natural-language or multimodal settings.
future_direction: Curriculum learning or reinforcement learning to steer models toward more compact reasoning.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis to uncover circuits for reasoning.
Extending the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off study to larger models and natural-language tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing highlight two key factors for improving reasoning in large language models (LLMs): (i) allocating more test-time compute tends to help on harder problems but often introduces redundancy in the reasoning trace, and (ii) compute is most effective when reasoning is systematic and incremental, forming structured chains of thought (CoTs) akin to human problem-solving. To study these factors in isolation, we introduce a controlled setting based on shortest-path tasks in layered graphs. We train decoder-only transformers on question-trace-answer triples using a custom tokenizer, comparing models trained on optimal bottom-up dynamic programming traces with those trained on longer, valid traces involving backtracking. Surprisingly, with the same training-token budget, models trained on inefficient traces generalize better to unseen graphs. This benefit is not due to length alone-injecting arbitrary redundancy into reasoning traces fails to help and can even hurt performance. Instead, we find that generalization correlates with the model's confidence in next-token prediction, suggesting that long, coherent, and locally incremental traces make the training signal easier to optimize.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: State over Tokens: Characterizing the Role of Reasoning Tokens
papers.research_question: What is the functional role of reasoning tokens in LLMs, given that they are not faithful explanations of the model's reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework, which reframes reasoning tokens as an externalized computational state that enables persistence across stateless generation cycles, explaining how they can drive correct reasoning without being faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens are best understood as an externalized computational state (SoT), which resolves misconceptions about their completeness and shared meaning, and opens new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning tokens are not faithful explanations of the model's internal reasoning process.
Reasoning tokens function as an externalized computational state (SoT), the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles.
The SoT view explains two common misconceptions: the misconception of completeness (tokens externalize only what is necessary for the next cycle) and the misconception of shared meaning (tokens may use model-specific encodings not interpretable by humans).
The tokens inhabit distinct ontological categories: as natural language text for human readers and as a computational substrate for the model.
The SoT framework surfaces new research questions about how LLMs encode and use state through tokens.
future_direction: How do LLMs decide what information to externalize at each cycle?
What information is actually encoded in the state at different points in the sequence?
Do they use consistent encodings across the solution of a problem and across different problems?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate reasoning tokens before their final answer to boost performance on complex tasks. While these sequences seem like human thought processes, empirical evidence reveals that they are not a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning process. To address this gap between appearance and function, we introduce the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework. SoT reframes reasoning tokens not as a linguistic narrative, but as an externalized computational state -- the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles. This explains how the tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation when read as text and surfaces previously overlooked research questions on these tokens. We argue that to truly understand the process that LLMs do, research must move beyond reading the reasoning tokens as text and focus on decoding them as state.

papers.title: Think-at-Hard: Selective Latent Iterations to Improve Reasoning Language Models
papers.research_question: Can LLMs selectively dedicate latent iterations only to hard tokens to improve reasoning capabilities under parameter constraints, avoiding latent overthinking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Think-at-Hard (TaH), a dynamic latent thinking method that selectively applies deeper iterations only to hard tokens, using duo-causal attention, depth-specific LoRA adapters, and a neural iteration decider, with a stable two-stage training scheme.
papers.conclusion: TaH establishes a new paradigm for improving reasoning within current parameter budgets by selectively iterating deeper only on hard tokens, achieving consistent gains with minimal overhead.
papers.key_findings:
TaH improves reasoning accuracy across five challenging math benchmarks by 4.0-5.4% over strong single-iteration baselines with minimal overhead (<3% extra parameters, ≈6% extra iterations).
Fixed-depth recurrent transformers suffer from latent overthinking, where easy tokens are incorrectly revised in additional iterations, harming performance.
An oracle policy that iterates only on incorrectly predicted tokens (hard tokens) shows substantial performance gains, validating the selective iteration approach.
The duo-causal attention mechanism enables cross-depth information flow while maintaining full sequential parallelism during training and inference.
The two-stage training scheme (first backbone with oracle policy, then decider imitation) stabilizes the training of the tightly coupled LLM backbone and iteration decider.
papers.limitation: Performance comparisons with official Qwen3 models are not direct because the official models use different training data distributions, scales, and procedures (including on-policy distillation), while TaH uses only SFT on limited public data.
future_direction: Integrating TaH with online distillation to provide stronger supervision.
Applying reinforcement learning to optimize the compute–accuracy trade-off and learn continuation policies beyond imitation.
papers.abstract: Improving reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), especially under parameter constraints, is crucial for real-world applications. Prior work proposes recurrent transformers, which allocate a fixed number of extra iterations per token to improve generation quality. After the first, standard forward pass, instead of verbalization, last-layer hidden states are fed back as inputs for additional iterations to refine token predictions. Yet we identify a latent overthinking phenomenon: easy token predictions that are already correct after the first pass are sometimes revised into errors in additional iterations. To address this, we propose Think-at-Hard (TaH), a dynamic latent thinking method that iterates deeper only at hard tokens. It employs a lightweight neural decider to trigger latent iterations only at tokens that are likely incorrect after the standard forward pass. During latent iterations, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules shift the LLM objective from general next-token prediction to focused hard-token refinement. We further introduce a duo-causal attention mechanism that extends attention from the token sequence dimension to an additional iteration depth dimension. This enables cross-iteration information flow while maintaining full sequential parallelism. Experiments show that TaH boosts LLM reasoning performance across five challenging benchmarks while maintaining the same parameter count. Compared with baselines that iterate twice for all output tokens, TaH delivers 8.1-11.3% accuracy gains while exempting 94% of tokens from the second iteration. Against strong single-iteration Qwen3 models finetuned with the same data, it also delivers 4.0-5.0% accuracy gains. When allowing less than 3% additional parameters from LoRA and the iteration decider, the gains increase to 8.5-12.6% and 5.3-5.4%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/TaH.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Improving Rule-based Reasoning in LLMs using Neurosymbolic Representations
papers.research_question: How can we improve rule-based reasoning in LLMs by encoding hidden states into neurosymbolic vectors and using symbolic algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurosymbolic method that encodes LLM hidden states into symbolic vectors, applies rule-based algorithms in the symbolic space, and decodes the results back, significantly improving performance on numerical reasoning tasks while maintaining generality.
papers.conclusion: The neurosymbolic method bridges the strengths of neural and symbolic reasoning, improving reliability, interpretability, and performance on rule-based tasks without sacrificing generality.
papers.key_findings:
The Neurosymbolic LLM outperforms standard LLM, CoT, and LoRA on mathematical reasoning tasks, with an average of 88.6% lower cross-entropy loss and 15.4 times more problems solved correctly.
The method does not degrade performance on out-of-distribution tasks (e.g., addition and integer division) due to a gating mechanism that avoids intervention for unfamiliar problem types.
Encoder performance is best at layer 17, indicating that middle layers optimally encode symbolic structure.
CoT reasoning introduces errors in multi-step reasoning, such as representation errors and infinite loops, leading to worse performance on some tasks compared to standard prompting.
LoRA fine-tuning improves some tasks but fails to generalize to unseen problem types, whereas the neurosymbolic method maintains generalization.
papers.limitation: Performance is lower on more complex tasks like LCM and square modulo due to the complexity of the underlying algorithms and the challenge of inserting neurosymbolic information via a single decoder network.
future_direction: Using multiple decoder networks to insert neurosymbolic information at different stages of the forward pass for more complex tasks.
Extending the method to other domains beyond mathematical reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) continue to face challenges in reliably solving reasoning tasks, particularly those that require precise rule following, as often found in mathematical reasoning. This paper introduces a novel neurosymbolic method that improves LLM reasoning by encoding hidden states into neurosymbolic vectors, enabling problem-solving within a neurosymbolic vector space. The results are decoded and merged with the original hidden state, significantly boosting the model's performance on numerical reasoning tasks. By offloading computation through neurosymbolic representations, this method enhances efficiency, reliability, and interpretability. Experimental results demonstrate an average of 88.6% lower cross-entropy loss and 15.4 times more problems correctly solved on a suite of mathematical reasoning tasks compared to chain-of-thought prompting and supervised fine-tuning (LoRA), without degrading performance on other tasks. We make our code available at: https://github.com/vdhanraj/Neurosymbolic-LLM.

papers.title: ThoughtProbe: Classifier-Guided Thought Space Exploration Leveraging LLM Intrinsic Reasoning
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities represented within LLMs’ internal activations, and how can these intrinsic abilities be effectively harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThoughtProbe, a classifier-guided search framework that leverages linear separability of thoughtfulness in LLM activations to improve reasoning performance without human intervention.
papers.conclusion: ThoughtProbe effectively leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities through classifier-guided exploration, advancing understanding and enabling practical application without human intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Thoughtfulness is linearly separable in LLMs' activation space, with a simple linear classifier achieving over 80% performance.
Different LLMs encode thoughtfulness differently across representation types and layers.
The classifier's logit consistently assigns higher scores to correct, thoughtful responses regardless of length.
The ThoughtProbe framework outperforms baselines on multiple math reasoning benchmarks.
Branch-aggregation selection outperforms single-branch selection and majority voting.
papers.limitation:
Fixed token lengths for segmenting intermediate thoughts may disrupt natural reasoning.
The gap between coverage and accuracy suggests room for improvement in answer selection.
Misalignment between training objectives (final outcomes) and guidance criteria (intermediate progress) may limit effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore more flexible, semantic-aware splitting criteria for tree node expansion.
Develop more sophisticated scoring metrics and aggregation methods for answer selection.
Explore step-wise feedback or hierarchical evaluation to better align classifier training.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have been demonstrated to possess intrinsic reasoning capabilities that can emerge naturally when expanding the response space. However, the neural representation mechanisms underlying these intrinsic capabilities and approaches for their optimal utilization remain inadequately understood. In this work, we make the key discovery that a simple linear classifier can effectively detect intrinsic reasoning capabilities in LLMs' activation space, particularly within specific representation types and network layers. Based on this finding, we propose a classifier-guided search framework that strategically explore a tree-structured response space. In each node expansion, the classifier serves as a scoring and ranking mechanism that efficiently allocates computational resources by identifying and prioritizing more thoughtful reasoning directions for continuation. After completing the tree expansion, we collect answers from all branches to form a candidate answer pool. We propose a branch-aggregation selection method that marginalizes over all supporting branches by aggregating their thoughtfulness scores, thereby identifying the optimal answer from the pool. Experimental results show that our framework's comprehensive exploration not only covers valid reasoning chains but also effectively identifies them, achieving significant improvements across multiple arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Semantic-level Internal Reasoning Graph
papers.research_question: How can faithfulness hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems be detected by capturing the model's internal reasoning processes at a semantic level?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a method that extends token-level Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to the semantic level to construct an internal reasoning graph for detecting faithfulness hallucinations in RAG systems, and introduces a framework that uses this graph to train a lightweight discriminator.
papers.conclusion: The proposed semantic-level internal reasoning graph method effectively detects faithfulness hallucinations by capturing the model's internal reasoning dependencies, and it outperforms existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method (SIRG) outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on RAGTruth and Dolly-15k datasets.
Faithfulness hallucinations arise when the model treats substantive fragments as linking fragments, leading to weaker dependency on the provided context.
The internal reasoning graph constructed by SIRG faithfully reflects the model's internal reasoning process, as validated by perturbation tests.
The method is more effective than token-level aggregation of attribution vectors (like LRP4RAG) because it filters out semantic noise.
The framework uses a small pre-trained language model (ALIGNSCORE) and achieves strong performance without multiple LLM invocations.
papers.abstract: The Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system based on Large language model (LLM) has made significant progress. It can effectively reduce factuality hallucinations, but faithfulness hallucinations still exist. Previous methods for detecting faithfulness hallucinations either neglect to capture the models' internal reasoning processes or handle those features coarsely, making it difficult for discriminators to learn. This paper proposes a semantic-level internal reasoning graph-based method for detecting faithfulness hallucination. Specifically, we first extend the layer-wise relevance propagation algorithm from the token level to the semantic level, constructing an internal reasoning graph based on attribution vectors. This provides a more faithful semantic-level representation of dependency. Furthermore, we design a general framework based on a small pre-trained language model to utilize the dependencies in LLM's reasoning for training and hallucination detection, which can dynamically adjust the pass rate of correct samples through a threshold. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves better overall performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on RAGTruth and Dolly-15k.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: A Statistical Physics of Language Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we model and understand the continuous-time reasoning dynamics of transformer language models using a statistical physics framework?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a statistical physics framework using stochastic differential equations and a Switching Linear Dynamical System to model and simulate reasoning dynamics in language models, enabling the prediction of misaligned states and failure modes.
papers.conclusion: The SLDS framework provides a tractable and interpretable model for reasoning dynamics, offering tools to study and predict critical transitions such as misaligned states in language models.
papers.key_findings:
A rank-40 projection captures 50% of the variance in sentence-level hidden state trajectories.
Four latent reasoning regimes are identified through Gaussian Mixture Model clustering of residuals.
The SLDS model accurately predicts reasoning dynamics and outperforms single-regime linear models in one-step-ahead prediction.
The framework shows transferability across models and tasks, though performance degrades across different model architectures.
In a case study, the SLDS successfully models and predicts adversarially induced belief shifts, demonstrating its utility for failure mode analysis.
future_direction: Future work could explore learning more invariant reasoning representations for better generalization.
papers.abstract: Transformer LMs show emergent reasoning that resists mechanistic understanding. We offer a statistical physics framework for continuous-time chain-of-thought reasoning dynamics. We model sentence-level hidden state trajectories as a stochastic dynamical system on a lower-dimensional manifold. This drift-diffusion system uses latent regime switching to capture diverse reasoning phases, including misaligned states or failures. Empirical trajectories (8 models, 7 benchmarks) show a rank-40 projection (balancing variance capture and feasibility) explains ~50% variance. We find four latent reasoning regimes. An SLDS model is formulated and validated to capture these features. The framework enables low-cost reasoning simulation, offering tools to study and predict critical transitions like misaligned states or other LM failures.

papers.title: States Hidden in Hidden States: LLMs Emerge Discrete State Representations Implicitly
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) form Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) during implicit consecutive addition tasks, and how are these representations formed and utilized?
papers.core_contribution: This paper discovers and analyzes Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) in LLMs, showing that models form and use these intermediate result representations to perform implicit consecutive addition without chain-of-thought.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) to perform implicit consecutive addition, providing insight into their multi-step reasoning and state-tracking abilities.
papers.key_findings:
IDSRs exist in the hidden states of LLMs during consecutive addition tasks, as confirmed by probing experiments.
IDSRs are formed independently for each digit and sequentially from the least significant digit, mirroring human calculation order.
A layer-wise transition occurs: early layers (0-50) contain linear IDSRs, middle layers (50-65) transition from linear to non-linear, and later layers (65-79) have non-linear features.
IDSRs are propagated along the sequence and used for subsequent calculations, as demonstrated by an attention bridge experiment.
The resolution of IDSRs degrades with sequence length, leading to inaccuracies in current open-source models.
papers.limitation:
Task diversity is limited; the hypothesis is validated only on a synthetic dataset of mathematical formulas.
Model diversity is limited; interpretability analysis requires open-source models, so experiments primarily use Qwen-72b, which has a capability gap compared to SOTA closed-source models.
future_direction: Investigate influence factors (e.g., training data, CoT) on the resolution of generated IDSRs.
Explore the underlying causes of the dynamic changes in IDSR properties (formation interpretability).
Study the patterns of IDSR generation across different model scales (scalability).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit various emergent abilities. Among these abilities, some might reveal the internal working mechanisms of models. In this paper, we uncover a novel emergent capability in models: the intrinsic ability to perform extended sequences of calculations without relying on chain-of-thought step-by-step solutions. Remarkably, the most advanced models can directly output the results of two-digit number additions with lengths extending up to 15 addends. We hypothesize that the model emerges Implicit Discrete State Representations (IDSRs) within its hidden states and performs symbolic calculations internally. To test this hypothesis, we design a sequence of experiments that look into the hidden states. Specifically, we first confirm that IDSRs exist. Then, we provide interesting observations about the formation of IDSRs from layer, digit, and sequence perspectives. Finally, we confirm that models indeed use IDSRs to produce the final answers. However, we also discover that these state representations are far from lossless in current open-sourced models, leading to inaccuracies in their final performance. Our work presents a novel exploration of LLMs' symbolic calculation abilities and the underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: ThinkLess: A Training-Free Inference-Efficient Method for Reducing Reasoning Redundancy
papers.abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves reasoning in large language models (LLMs), the excessive length of reasoning tokens increases latency and KV cache memory usage, and may even truncate final answers under context limits. We propose ThinkLess, an inference-efficient framework that terminates reasoning generation early and maintains output quality without modifying the model. Atttention analysis reveals that answer tokens focus minimally on earlier reasoning steps and primarily attend to the reasoning terminator token, due to information migration under causal masking. Building on this insight, ThinkLess inserts the terminator token at earlier positions to skip redundant reasoning while preserving the underlying knowledge transfer. To prevent format discruption casued by early termination, ThinkLess employs a lightweight post-regulation mechanism, relying on the model's natural instruction-following ability to produce well-structured answers. Without fine-tuning or auxiliary data, ThinkLess achieves comparable accuracy to full-length CoT decoding while greatly reducing decoding time and memory consumption.

papers.title: Learning to Disentangle Latent Reasoning Rules with Language VAEs: A Systematic Study
papers.research_question: How can reasoning rules be explicitly encoded within the latent space of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a complete pipeline for learning reasoning rules within Transformer-based language VAEs, encompassing three rule-based reasoning tasks, a supporting theoretical framework based on Neural Tangent Kernel theory, and a practical end-to-end architecture.
papers.conclusion: This work serves as a foundational step in exploring rule-based representation learning under the language VAE architecture for NLI tasks, demonstrating that reasoning rules can be disentangled in the encoder's parametric space and that injecting latent reasoning representations into the decoder's query improves performance.
papers.key_findings:
Under explicit signal supervision, reasoning rules can be disentangled within the encoder’s parametric space, resulting in distinct clustering of rules in the output feature space.
Injecting reasoning information into the Query of the attention mechanism enables the model to more effectively retrieve the stored Value from memory based on Key, offering a simple method for integrating prior knowledge into decoder-only language models.
FFN layers are better than attention layers at preserving the separation of reasoning rules in the model’s parameters.
Increasing the number of training samples per operation beyond a threshold (around 2000) leads to a decline in accuracy, indicating an information bottleneck where models rely on memorization rather than rule-based reasoning.
Integrating BM25-based sample selection during training yields enhanced performance, indicating the effectiveness of relevance-guided sampling.
papers.limitation: This study does not aim to explore rule composition or generalisation.
future_direction: Investigation of diffusion-based language models, such as Mmada, to improve flexibility for constraining the decoding process.
papers.abstract: Incorporating explicit reasoning rules within the latent space of language models (LMs) offers a promising pathway to enhance generalisation, interpretability, and controllability. While current Transformer-based language models have shown strong performance on Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks, they often rely on memorisation rather than rule-based inference. This work investigates how reasoning rules can be explicitly embedded and memorised within the LMs through Language Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). We propose a complete pipeline for learning reasoning rules within Transformer-based language VAEs. This pipeline encompasses three rule-based reasoning tasks, a supporting theoretical framework, and a practical end-to-end architecture. The experiment illustrates the following findings: Disentangled reasoning: Under explicit signal supervision, reasoning rules - viewed as functional mappings - can be disentangled within the encoder's parametric space. This separation results in distinct clustering of rules in the output feature space. Prior knowledge injection: injecting reasoning information into the Query enables the model to more effectively retrieve the stored value Value from memory based on Key. This approach offers a simple method for integrating prior knowledge into decoder-only language models. Performance bottleneck: In mathematical reasoning tasks using Qwen2.5(0.5B), increasing sample count doesn't improve performance beyond a point. Moreover, ffn layers are better than attention layers at preserving the separation of reasoning rules in the model's parameters.

papers.title: Bottom-up Policy Optimization: Your Language Model Policy Secretly Contains Internal Policies
papers.research_question: How does internal reasoning evolve through the layers and modules of a language model, and can this understanding be used to improve reinforcement learning optimization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to decompose an LLM's policy into internal layer and modular policies via the residual stream, reveals distinct reasoning patterns across model families, and proposes a novel RL paradigm (BuPO) that optimizes these internal policies from the bottom up to improve reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that decomposing language model policies into internal components reveals systematic reasoning patterns and that bottom-up optimization of these internal policies is an effective reinforcement learning paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Language model policies can be decomposed into internal layer and modular policies via the residual stream, revealing distinct reasoning roles.
A universal reasoning structure exists: early layers maintain high entropy for exploration, while top layers converge to near-zero entropy for final prediction.
Qwen models exhibit a progressive, human-like reasoning pattern (Exploration-Integration-Convergence), while Llama models show abrupt convergence only in the final layers.
Optimizing internal layer policies induces feature refinement, forcing lower layers to preemptively capture high-level reasoning representations.
The proposed Bottom-up Policy Optimization (BuPO) method, which aligns internal policies early in training, outperforms conventional RL baselines on complex reasoning benchmarks.
papers.limitation: Excessive training steps for the internal policy lead to model collapse, indicating a trade-off and the need for moderate optimization.
future_direction: Understanding how internal reasoning patterns emerge remains an important direction for future work.
The selection and investigation of internal policies remain promising directions for future research.
papers.abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches treat large language models (LLMs) as a unified policy, overlooking their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we decompose the LLM-based policy into Internal Layer Policies and Internal Modular Policies via Transformer's residual stream. Our entropy analysis on internal policy reveals distinct patterns: (1) universally, policies evolve from high-entropy exploration in early layers to deterministic refinement in top layers; and (2) Qwen exhibits a progressive, human-like reasoning structure, contrasting with the abrupt final-layer convergence in Llama. Furthermore, we discover that optimizing internal layers induces feature refinement, forcing lower layers to capture high-level reasoning representations early. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bottom-up Policy Optimization (BuPO), a novel RL paradigm that reconstructs the LLM's reasoning foundation from the bottom up by optimizing internal layers in early stages. Extensive experiments on complex reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of BuPO. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/BuPO.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: ActivationReasoning: Logical Reasoning in Latent Activation Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we embed explicit logical reasoning into the latent space of LLMs to improve transparency, controllability, and reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACTIVATIONREASONING (AR), a framework that embeds logical reasoning into the latent space of LLMs by treating SAE features as propositions and composing them through explicit rules, improving transparency, robustness, and control.
papers.conclusion: AR unifies the semantic richness of LLMs with the systematic generalization of logic, moving toward models that can reason more robustly and operate in closer alignment with human values.
papers.key_findings:
AR improves multi-hop reasoning and scales robustly with reasoning complexity.
AR generalizes to abstract and context-sensitive tasks, such as safety and meta-level concept descriptions.
AR transfers across model backbones (Llama and Gemma).
AR outperforms baseline models and instruction-tuned variants on multiple benchmarks.
AR enables fine-grained inspection and control of model behavior through latent activations.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on SAEs, which may have limitations in capturing higher-level abstractions and are subject to polysemy and context dependence.
Real-world reasoning challenges can become more diverse than the tasks highlighted, including open-ended reasoning, long-context inference, or knowledge-intensive domains.
Manual or semi-automatic rule definition and concept identification.
Purely deductive reasoning; does not handle uncertainty.
future_direction: Automatic rule discovery and integration with probabilistic or inductive reasoning modules.
Automatic selection of concept representation types (single/multi/relational).
Extending AR to multimodal settings (e.g., vision or VLMs) using multimodal SAEs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, but their internal reasoning remains opaque and difficult to control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) make hidden activations more interpretable by exposing latent features that often align with human concepts. Yet, these features are fragile and passive, offering no mechanism for systematic reasoning or model control. To address this, we introduce ActivationReasoning (AR), a framework that embeds explicit logical reasoning into the latent space of LLMs. It proceeds in three stages: (1) Finding latent representations, first latent concept representations are identified (e.g., via SAEs) and organized into a dictionary; (2) Activating propositions, at inference time AR detects activating concepts and maps them to logical propositions; and (3)Logical reasoning, applying logical rules over these propositions to infer higher-order structures, compose new concepts, and steer model behavior. We evaluate AR on multi-hop reasoning (PrOntoQA), abstraction and robustness to indirect concept cues (Rail2Country), reasoning over natural and diverse language (ProverQA), and context-sensitive safety (BeaverTails). Across all tasks, AR scales robustly with reasoning complexity, generalizes to abstract and context-sensitive tasks, and transfers across model backbones. These results demonstrate that grounding logical structure in latent activations not only improves transparency but also enables structured reasoning, reliable control, and alignment with desired behaviors, providing a path toward more reliable and auditable AI.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance.
